Apex Industrial Equipment - Q3 FY2024 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Industrial Equipment Q3 FY2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are in listen-only mode. After the presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. If you would like to ask a question at that time, please press star then one on your touchtone phone. If you're using a speakerphone, please pick up your handset before pressing the keys. To withdraw your question, press star then two. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson (Head of Investor Relations):
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss Apex Industrial Equipment's results for the Q3 FY2024. Joining me on today's call are Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; and Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking in nature and subject to certain risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Mike Thompson.

Mike Thompson (CEO):
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. I'm pleased to report on Apex Industrial Equipment's performance for the Q3 ended September 30, 2024. We've made significant progress on several fronts, delivering strong results amid a dynamic industrial landscape marked by reshoring trends, automation demand, and energy transition tailwinds. We've seen robust total order intake of $2.85 billion, up 18% year-over-year, reflecting solid customer confidence in our CNC machining centers, robotic systems, and material handling solutions. Lead times for key products and components have improved meaningfully, enhancing our operational agility and customer satisfaction. We've executed effectively on our share repurchase program, deploying capital opportunistically to boost shareholder value. And strategically, we've advanced our M&A pipeline with key acquisitions that bolster our capabilities in cobots and precision forgings.

We are confident that our strategic initiatives—centered on Industry 4.0 integration, supply chain resilience, and electrification—are positioning us for long-term sustainable growth.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Lisa to provide more detail on our financial results.

Lisa Chen (CFO):
Thank you, Mike. Turning to our financial performance, Apex Industrial Equipment reported $2.65 billion in revenue for the quarter, representing a 15% increase year-over-year. Gross margin expanded to 39%, driven by a favorable product mix shift toward high-margin automation and digital services, along with pricing discipline and procurement savings from diversified sourcing. Operating expenses were $520 million, reflecting targeted investments in R&D for our ApexEdge IoT platform and sales expansion in reshoring markets. This resulted in operating income of $425 million. Our net income for the quarter was $320 million, or $0.92 per diluted share.

We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet, with $1.2 billion in cash and cash equivalents, providing flexibility for growth investments, dividends, and buybacks. Net leverage stands at a healthy 1.2x EBITDA.

Good afternoon, everyone—thank you for joining our Q3 earnings call. I'll dive right into our order intake performance, which continues to be a bright spot and a strong leading indicator for our future revenue stream here at Apex Industrial Equipment. As you know, in the manufacturing and industrial equipment sector, order intake reflects not just current demand but customer confidence in capex cycles, supply chain stability, and our value proposition in delivering mission-critical solutions like CNC machining centers, robotic automation systems, and heavy-duty material handling equipment.

For the third quarter ended September 30, 2024, total order intake reached $2.85 billion, marking a robust 18% year-over-year increase from $2.42 billion in Q3 FY2023. This exceeded our internal guidance midpoint of $2.7 billion and came in above the Street consensus of $2.75 billion. On a constant currency basis, the growth was even stronger at 20%, underscoring genuine underlying demand rather than FX tailwinds.

Let me break this down for you across our key segments, as visibility here helps frame the sustainability of this momentum. Our Discrete Automation segment—think high-precision CNC lathes, milling machines, and factory floor robotics akin to what Fanuc or Haas Automation dominate—saw orders of $1.25 billion, up 25% YoY. This was fueled by surging demand from semiconductor fab expansions and EV battery gigafactory builds. Customers like TSMC and Tesla suppliers are ramping up, and our next-gen ApexFlex robotic arms with integrated AI vision systems have been a standout, capturing 15% market share in sub-10kg payload collaborative robots.

Process Industries, which includes our large-scale pumps, valves, and distillation columns for oil & gas, chemicals, and renewables—similar to Flowserve or Sulzer offerings—posted $850 million in orders, a solid 12% YoY growth. Here, the energy transition is playing out vividly: LNG infrastructure projects in the U.S. Gulf Coast and Qatar drove 30% of this segment's intake, while our low-emission turbomachinery for green hydrogen plants secured landmark deals totaling $150 million.

Motion and Drives rounded out at $750 million, up 10% YoY, with strength in variable frequency drives (VFDs) and servo motors for warehouse automation. The e-commerce boom post-Amazon's fulfillment center expansions has been a tailwind, much like peers ABB and Rockwell Automation have reported.

Regionally, the story is equally compelling. North America accounted for 48% of intake at $1.37 billion, surging 28% YoY. Reshoring and the CHIPS Act are accelerating domestic manufacturing: we've seen pull-forward from automotive OEMs like Ford and GM for aluminum die-casting equipment tied to their F-150 Lightning EV lines, plus a $200 million book of business from data center HVAC giants amid hyperscaler capex. Book-to-bill in the region hit 1.35x, with backlog now at $4.2 billion—up 22% YoY.

EMEA contributed 32% or $913 million, up 15% YoY despite softer German auto output. Strength came from wind turbine nacelle tooling for Vestas and Siemens Gamesa suppliers, and our sustainable coolant systems for European machine shops compliant with the EU's Green Deal regs. UK and Nordic infra spend offset French election jitters.

Asia-Pacific was 20% at $570 million, growing 8% YoY on a tough comp from last year's post-COVID surge. China semi equipment restrictions bit us here—orders dipped 5%—but India and Southeast Asia more than compensated, with $120 million in orders for textile machinery upgrades and solar panel production lines. Our partnerships with Foxconn for Apple supply chain automation are yielding early wins.

Now, zooming out to trends and strategic insights: Our trailing 12-month book-to-bill ratio stands at 1.22x, well above the industry benchmark of 1.1x seen at peers like Caterpillar or Illinois Tool Works. This has ballooned our total backlog to a record $9.8 billion, up 24% YoY, providing exceptional revenue visibility—over 70% of next year's topline is now locked in. Conversion timing remains healthy at 85% within 12 months, though lead times for high-complexity systems like our ApexForge 5-axis CNC mills have stretched to 9-12 months due to specialized steel castings and chip shortages easing slower than expected.

Driving this isn't luck—it's execution on technical initiatives. We've accelerated our Industry 4.0 roadmap: 60% of Q3 orders included our ApexEdge IoT platform, which integrates edge computing for predictive maintenance, reducing unplanned downtime by 25% per customer pilots. Margins here are juicy—digital services attach at 20% of hardware ASPs with 70% gross margins. Electrification is another pillar: our EV-neutral e-axle test stands and battery assembly lines captured 40% of Discrete orders, positioning us ahead of rivals like Dürr or Brooks Automation in the $50 billion addressable megatrend.

Strategically, we're leaner and meaner: supply chain diversification—now 40% North American sourcing vs. 25% two years ago—shielded us from Red Sea disruptions, keeping COGS flat QoQ. We're guiding FY2024 total order intake to $11.2-11.5 billion, implying 16-19% growth, with Q4 seasonality tempered by holiday factory shutdowns but offset by year-end capex pushes.

Risks? Sticky inflation in alloys and skilled labor could pressure mix if low-margin commodity equipment rebounds. Geopolitics in Asia looms, but our 35% exposure with hedging mitigates. Upside? U.S. infra bill Phase 2 and EU NextGenEU disbursements could juice Q1 '25.

In summary, this 18% YoY order growth validates our leadership in industrial equipment amid capex normalization. We're not just riding the cycle—we're shaping it through innovation and customer intimacy.

Before moving on, I'd like to touch on another critical operational metric we've been tracking closely: lead times for our key products and components. In our sector—where we're competing head-to-head with the likes of Caterpillar, Siemens, and Fanuc—lead times serve as a barometer of supply chain health, customer satisfaction, and our pricing power. Shortening them not only accelerates revenue recognition from our $9.8 billion backlog but also supports our book-to-bill ratio, which came in at 1.22x this quarter.

The headline is positive: average lead times across our core product portfolio have improved sequentially by 22% quarter-over-quarter, now at 16 weeks, down from a pandemic-era peak of 28 weeks in Q3 2022. Year-over-year, that's a 35% reduction. For our flagship offerings—like our Precision CNC machining centers and modular robotic automation systems used in automotive and aerospace assembly lines—lead times have compressed to 12-14 weeks, giving us a competitive edge over peers still quoting 18-20 weeks. This is particularly evident in our high-margin ServoDrive series robotic arms, where we've cut lead times from 20 weeks to just 10 weeks, thanks to ramped production at our new Greenville, South Carolina facility.

Breaking it down by product category: Discrete Automation Equipment (35% of revenue): Lead times for our Fanuc-compatible six-axis robots and collaborative cobots are now at 11 weeks, a 40% improvement YoY. This reflects better throughput on our assembly lines, where we've implemented AI-driven predictive maintenance via our proprietary Apex Nexus platform, reducing unplanned downtime by 28%.

Heavy Machinery (45% of revenue): For hydraulic presses and forging equipment akin to those supplied to John Deere's ag implement lines, we're at 18 weeks—still elevated due to steel casting constraints but down 25% QoQ. Our custom turbine housings for wind energy OEMs like Vestas have seen the biggest gains, dropping to 15 weeks after qualifying new domestic foundry partners.

Components and Sub-Assemblies (20% of revenue): Critical inputs like high-precision roller bearings from suppliers mirroring SKF and Timken are now at 8 weeks, a 50% cut YoY, aided by our strategic inventory build to 14 weeks of forward coverage. However, semiconductor-based PLC controls and variable frequency drives—think Siemens SIMATIC equivalents—are lingering at 18 weeks due to ongoing fab capacity tightness at TSMC and Infineon. Rare earth magnets for our permanent magnet synchronous motors (PMSMs) have stabilized at 12 weeks after diversifying away from 70% China-sourced supply to include Australian and U.S. miners like Lynas and MP Materials.

Regionally: North America (52% of orders): Lead times here are our best at 13 weeks on average, buoyed by nearshoring trends and the CHIPS Act incentives. Our Mexico City expansion—adding 200,000 sq ft for CNC final assembly—has slashed trans-Pacific shipping risks, with 85% of U.S. customer orders now fulfilled under 12 weeks.

EMEA (28% of orders): More challenged at 19 weeks, pressured by Red Sea disruptions adding 2-3 weeks to component ocean freight and elevated energy costs impacting European steel mills. That said, we've locked in 18-month take-or-pay contracts with ThyssenKrupp for alloy steels, which should bring this down to 16 weeks by Q4.

Asia-Pacific (20% of orders): At 15 weeks, this region's booming semiconductor fab builds—think TSMC's Japan and U.S. expansions—are driving demand for our wafer handling robots, but port congestion in Shanghai has kept components sticky. Our new Singapore stocking hub is mitigating this, with JIT kanban replenishment cutting intra-Asia lead times by 30%.

On the technical front, these improvements stem from $150 million invested over the last 18 months in supply chain digitization: deploying digital twin simulations with Siemens NX software to model end-to-end throughput, and rolling out SAP S/4HANA-integrated AI forecasting that has improved demand signal accuracy by 42%, reducing safety stock needs by 15%. We've also vertically integrated 25% of our electronics board assembly in-house at our Ohio campus, derisking against the ongoing global chip shortage that's still hampering competitors like Rockwell Automation.

Strategically, shorter lead times are translating to real financial upside. We're seeing pull-forward of orders—backlog grew 24% YoY—and pricing discipline, with a 4.2% ASP increase on new automation deals due to allocation premiums. Looking ahead, we expect further compression to 14 weeks enterprise-wide by year-end, assuming no major escalations in U.S.-China trade tensions or Baltic Dry Index spikes. To sustain this, we're committing another $200 million to capacity: a second cobot line in Vietnam for APAC and advanced composites tooling in Germany to support the EU's Green Deal push for lighter industrial gear.

In short, our lead time trajectory underscores Apex's operational resilience in a volatile macro environment—supply chains are stabilizing, but we're not complacent. This positions us to capture market share as capex cycles turn in autos, renewables, and semiconductors.

Turning to capital allocation, I'd like to provide a detailed update on our share repurchase program, which remains a cornerstone of our disciplined framework in this cyclical industry. The industrial equipment sector has navigated a choppy landscape this year—persistent supply chain headwinds from Red Sea disruptions, softening industrial capex in China amid their property sector woes, and robust reshoring tailwinds in North America driven by the CHIPS Act and IRA incentives. Amid these dynamics, our $1.5 billion authorization, announced in February 2023 following our Investor Day, underscores our confidence in Apex's long-term value creation as a leader in CNC machining centers, hydraulic systems, and next-gen automation platforms like our ApexFlex robotic arms.

To date, we've repurchased approximately 28.7 million shares, or 62% of our authorization, for a total of $932 million. This includes $285 million deployed in Q3 alone, at an average price of $32.47 per share—well below our current trading multiple of 14.2x forward EPS and our five-year average of 17.8x. Year-to-date through Q3, the average repurchase price stands at $32.51, representing a 22% discount to our year-end 2023 closing price of $41.62 and a compelling 18% below our intrinsic value estimate derived from our DCF model incorporating 8-10% organic revenue CAGR through 2028, fueled by automation adoption and electrification retrofits in heavy machinery.

Execution has been opportunistic and Rule 10b5-1 compliant, leveraging automated trading plans to minimize market impact. We accelerated repurchases in Q3 by 35% quarter-over-quarter, capitalizing on the 15% share price drawdown from mid-year peaks, triggered by broader industrials weakness amid high interest rates and delayed capex decisions from OEMs like those in ag equipment and off-highway vehicles—think peers like Deere & Company facing similar inventory destocking. We've sourced funding primarily from our robust free cash flow generation, which hit $425 million YTD, up 12% from prior year, supported by 9% operating margins in our core hydraulics and precision tooling segments. No incremental debt was drawn; our net leverage remains at a pristine 1.2x EBITDA, giving us ample dry powder.

Regionally, this ties directly into our market positioning. In North America, which accounts for 58% of our revenue, reshoring has boosted aftermarket demand for our high-margin spindle rebuild kits and IoT-enabled predictive maintenance solutions, allowing us to deploy 45% of Q3 buybacks here via efficient block trades. EMEA repurchases were more measured at 25% of volume, reflecting energy cost volatility impacting capex for wind turbine manufacturers—similar to challenges at Siemens Energy. APAC, at 30%, benefited from targeted open-market purchases during lulls in Shanghai trading hours, hedging against yen weakness that pressured Japanese OEMs like Komatsu.

Strategically, this program is accretive on multiple fronts. Post-execution, we've reduced diluted shares outstanding by 4.2% YTD to 412 million, directly boosting adjusted EPS by $0.28, or 7%, all else equal—key in a sector where EPS visibility is prized amid lumpy order books. ROIC remains above our 12% WACC hurdle, with buybacks yielding an IRR north of 15% based on current valuations. Looking forward, we have $568 million remaining under authorization, with no fixed cadence but a bias toward continued deployment in H2 if shares trade below 15x forward earnings. This complements our $300 million annual dividend, targeting a 40/60 split between dividends and buybacks, while preserving balance sheet flexibility for M&A tuck-ins like our recent $150 million acquisition of a German servo-motor fab to bolster EV drivetrain capabilities.

In summary, our repurchase execution exemplifies Apex's shareholder-friendly ethos in an industry shifting toward automation and sustainability megatrends. We're not chasing headlines; we're methodically enhancing per-share value amid peers like Ingersoll Rand and Parker Hannifin who've similarly leaned into buybacks during valuation dislocations.

Finally, I'll turn to our M&A activity, which has been a cornerstone of our strategy to accelerate growth in the industrial equipment sector amid ongoing supply chain disruptions, the push toward Industry 4.0, and the electrification megatrend. As you know, the global industrial machinery market is projected to grow at a 5.2% CAGR through 2028, per recent McKinsey data, driven by automation demand in automotive, aerospace, and renewables. However, with macroeconomic headwinds like persistent inflation in raw materials—up 12% YoY for steel and aluminum—and geopolitical tensions affecting 30% of our Asia-Pacific supply base, we've been disciplined in pursuing bolt-on acquisitions that enhance our core competencies in CNC machining centers, material handling systems, and precision robotics.

In Q3, we closed two transformative deals totaling $725 million, funded through a mix of cash on hand—$1.2 billion at quarter-end—and $400 million in low-cost term debt at 4.2% via our revolving credit facility. These represent a 15% increase in our annual M&A spend from 2023, aligning with the sector's 22% YoY uptick in deal volume as tracked by PwC's industrials M&A report.

First, our $450 million acquisition of EuroTech Robotics, a Germany-based leader in collaborative robots—or cobots—for automotive assembly lines. EuroTech brings 250 employees, €120 million in trailing twelve-month revenue (about 18% of which is recurring from software subscriptions), and a 12% EBITDA margin. This deal is immediately accretive, adding 25 cents to FY24 EPS, with full-year run-rate synergies of $65 million by Year 2, primarily from cross-selling our servo motors and PLC controls into their 5,000-unit installed base. Strategically, it positions us to capture the cobot market's 28% CAGR, fueled by labor shortages in Europe and North America—U.S. manufacturing PMI labor diffusion index hit 55 in September, signaling tightness. We've already integrated their KUKA-compatible APIs with our ApexEdge IoT platform, enabling predictive maintenance that reduces downtime by 22% in pilot programs with Ford and Volkswagen suppliers. Regionally, this shores up our EMEA exposure, where we've grown 14% YoY to $2.1 billion, offsetting softness in China due to EV overcapacity and U.S. tariffs on imported equipment.

Second, the $275 million tuck-in of PrecisionForge Components, a U.S. Midwest fabricator specializing in lightweight aluminum die-castings for electric vehicle powertrains and aerospace turbine housings. With $85 million in revenue and a robust 14% organic growth profile tied to Boeing and Tesla's supply chains, this acquisition diversifies our $3.8 billion forgings and castings segment, which faced 8% margin compression from steel price volatility. Synergies here total $35 million annually, driven by 20% procurement savings via our global scale—think leveraging our long-term contracts with Nucor for aluminum at 15% below spot—and capacity optimization at our Ohio facility, boosting utilization from 72% to 88%. This move supports reshoring trends: U.S. industrial equipment capex is up 11% YoY per ISM data, with 40% directed toward domestic suppliers amid CHIPS Act funding for semis and IRA incentives for EV battery plants.

Looking broader, our M&A pipeline remains robust at $2.5 billion, focused on three pillars: (1) Digital transformation, targeting firms with AI-driven edge computing like our interest in complementing Rockwell Automation-inspired software stacks; (2) Sustainability, pursuing green tech such as hydrogen-compatible welding systems to meet EU CBAM tariffs starting 2026; and (3) Geographic resilience, with selective Asia bets outside China—e.g., India and Vietnam, where industrial equipment demand is surging 19% amid "China+1" shifts. We've divested two non-core legacy assets for $150 million, including a low-margin hydraulic press line, yielding a 2.1x MOIC and redeploying capital at 18% IRR hurdles.

These initiatives de-risk our 10-12% mid-term EBITDA margins while driving 7-9% organic revenue growth. Forward-looking, we expect M&A to contribute 20% of our FY25 topline expansion, positioning Apex Industrial Equipment as a pure-play leader against peers like Caterpillar in earthmoving or Siemens in factory automation.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star then one on your touchtone phone. Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Smith (Goldman Sachs):
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the demand environment you're seeing in the industrial automation market?

Mike Thompson (CEO):
Good morning, John. Thanks for the question. Demand in industrial automation remains robust, particularly in Discrete Automation, where we saw $1.25 billion in orders, up 25% year-over-year. Semiconductor expansions and EV gigafactories are key drivers—think TSMC ramps and Tesla suppliers betting big on our ApexFlex robotic arms, which now hold 15% share in collaborative robots under 10kg payload. North America led with 28% growth, fueled by reshoring and CHIPS Act-related capex. Even in EMEA and APAC, we're gaining traction with partnerships like Foxconn for supply chain automation. Book-to-bill at 1.22x trailing 12 months gives us great visibility, and 60% of orders included ApexEdge IoT for predictive maintenance. We're optimistic as capex cycles normalize.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Davis with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Emily Davis (JPMorgan):
What are your expectations for capital expenditures in the coming year?

Lisa Chen (CFO):
Thanks, Emily. For FY2025, we're guiding capex to $450-500 million, up modestly from $420 million this year, representing about 3% of revenue. This focuses on high-ROI areas: $200 million for supply chain capacity like our Vietnam cobot line and Germany composites tooling to further compress lead times; $150 million in digital twins and AI forecasting to sustain 42% better demand accuracy; and the balance for facility expansions in Mexico City and Ohio to support reshoring. These investments yield quick payback—our recent Greenville ramp cut robotic arm lead times to 10 weeks—and align with 70% backlog visibility into next year. We'll fund from free cash flow, maintaining leverage below 1.5x.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Robert Lee with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Robert Lee (Barclays):
How are you managing supply chain disruptions, and what impact are they having on your margins?

Mike Thompson (CEO):
Hi Robert, good question. We've made supply chain resilience a top priority, diversifying to 40% North American sourcing from 25% two years ago, which insulated us from Red Sea issues—COGS stayed flat QoQ. Lead times improved 22% sequentially to 16 weeks average, with components like bearings at 8 weeks via 14-week inventory buffers and new foundry partners. For semis and PLCs, still at 18 weeks due to fab tightness, but in-house electronics assembly covers 25%. Margins benefited—gross at 39%—from mix shift to automation, 4.2% ASP hikes on premiums, and procurement savings. No major margin hit; we're guiding stable 38-40% through FY25 as disruptions ease.

Operator:
Thank you. There are no further questions at this time.

Mike Thompson (CEO):
Thank you for your questions and your interest in Apex Industrial Equipment. We are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our strategy and delivering long-term value for our shareholders.

Sarah Johnson (Head of Investor Relations):
Thank you, everyone, for joining us today. This concludes our earnings call. Have a great day.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
